newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Ecu bonds to retain risks on road to EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ecu bonds to retain risks on road to EMU.

text.p: On the face of it, Ecu government bonds seem like the perfect route to invest in bonds denominated in the new single currency.
But analysts said there are a number of risks during the road to European economic and monetary union (EMU) and as a result Ecu paper will still hold a yield premium over Bunds.

Ecu-denominated 10-year French government bond yields are more than 30 basis points above equivalent yields on French and German government bonds but analysts say even if monetary union becomes a certainty, the disparity is probably justified.

Bonds denominated in Ecu, a basket of 12 European currencies, are due to be paid back in euros, likely to be worth more since it will exclude weaker economies not yet ready for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). But that is not enough.
Analysts say doubt about which countries will join a single currency and at what exchange rates their currencies will be converted into the euro leaves an element of risk.

What's more, the Ecu market remains starved of liquidity. Only France and Britain have regular Ecu issuance programmes, and even the French market lacks sufficient issues to give efficient pricing along the yield curve.
"The recent news has been clearly bullish for convergence, but there's little incentive for the market to narrow the spread to zero just yet," said Steve Major, head bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais.
"Lack of liquidity, uncertainty regarding exactly which countries will be at stage three (the launch of EMU) and at what conversion rates provide the reason for the spread," he said.

These factors outweigh optimism that EMU will start on schedule in 1999, encouraged by a meeting in Dublin in September where finance ministers reached broad agreement on some of the main issues still to be resolved.
CONVERGENCE TRADES A PROBLEM

Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN-AMRO in Paris, said he was sceptical about using Ecu bonds for European monetary union convergence plays because of the complexities involved in deriving a fair value for Ecu bonds.
Convergence trades bet on the view that bond yields will come closer together as countries align their economies to meet Maastricht Treaty criteria.

For each of the 12 members which make up the Ecu basket, Brossard said investors need to assess the probability of entry into the single currency, how much yield can be picked up and the potential currency gains or losses.
"You can work out the theoretical value based on which countries are likely to enter but the day before EMU, the Ecu is a basket and the day after it's something completely different," he said.

"And if you want to buy a basket, then don't buy a ready made one, make your own and make sure it's a liquid one," Brossard said. "If you think Italy's going to be in EMU don't buy a piece of Italy, buy Italy."
FRENCH INITIATIVE
In France, however, the assurance by the government that its bonds will be repaid in euros is enticing some investors.

Analysts say domestic institutions are buying Ecu OATs to cover future payments they have to make to investors after the introduction of the euro simply because the nominal yield is higher than that on French franc OATs.

"Investors increasingly evaluate Ecu OATs, not against a theoretical Ecu basket of up to 12 members, but against French franc OATs -- they have the same credit and France is guaranteeing conversion into euros," Ciaran O'Hagan, bond analyst at JP Morgan in Paris, said.
For the investor needing to assess continually the value of portfolios on current values there may be difficulties unless the currency risk is hedged, said O'Hagan.

Comparing nominal Ecu yields to Bund yields, Brossard said, "The only problem is we do not know at which Ecu/mark exchange rate (EMU) will happen, so it is not clear whether the current Ecu-Bund spread is enough to offset any currency risk."
The French government has tried hard to boost the Ecu market, albeit with an ulterior motive of cornering the market in euro-denominated bonds for Paris after 1999.
"But they need other countries to take the plunge," said Major at Credit Lyonnais. "The ultimate signal of the arrival of the Ecu-euro market would be a German issue," he said.
SCARCE ECU ISSUANCE

Ecu issuance by non-sovereign borrowers has all but dried up since the Danish rejection of the Maastricht treaty in June 1992 destroyed confidence in a smooth path to monetary union and dealt a body-blow the to Ecu market.

According to figures from Capital DATA Bondware total international Ecu bond issuance so far in 1996 amounts to a paltry 2.865 billion Ecu ($3.58 billion). That's a tenth of the amount issued in the 1991, the Ecu's champagne year.
Half of all international Ecu bond issues during the past 15 years came between 1990 and 1992. In 1991 the Ecu market was second only to the dollar as a source of funds.

The most significant Ecu issue this year was the European Investment Bank's sale in March of 500 million Ecu Eurobonds, with a first ever definitive clause in the prospectus assuring a one-for-one convertibility with the euro.

Jean-Marc Debricon at the European Bank of Research and Development's treasury department said the issue helped pave the way for its own Ecu issue in July, which also included a definitive one-for-one clause.
He said, however, that while there was demand for its relatively small Ecu issue from investors the EBRD would be unlikely to come to the market with a large, liquid deal.
"There is demand from retail (investors), but why come up with a 400-500 million Ecu deal?" said Debricon.
The one-for-one clause included by the EIB and EBRD was designed to assuage lingering concerns about the continuity of Ecu contracts when the euro is introduced.
Analysts said while it has taken some time for European governments to hammer the point home, it is becoming accepted that the legal status of the euro will ensure the continuity of Ecu contracts.
A paper prepared by the European Commission is expected to be put forward later this month and formally adopted in December at a summit of EU leaders.
"It's a done deal, the only thing to be settled is the wording of the regulation," said Jonathan Davies, bond analyst at UBS Ltd in London. "It will be difficult for any lawyer to wriggle out of it."
